name: Cradle Mountain
tagline: Jagged dolerite peaks, glacial lakes and wombats in Tasmania's best-known World Heritage park.
description: Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park sits in the Central Highlands, with the Cradle Mountain end in the north and Lake St Clair in the south. People come to walk among alpine heath, button-grass plains and rainforest, from short boardwalks to the multi-day Overland Track. Gustav Weindorfer built a chalet here in 1912 and campaigned for the area to become a national park for everyone. Wombats, wallabies and pademelons graze near the tracks, and the weather can turn cold and wet at any time of year.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass needed
goodToKnow.detail: A valid Tasmanian parks pass is required to enter the national park; check current pass options on the Parks and Wildlife Service site before you arrive.

goodToKnow.title: Book the Overland Track
goodToKnow.detail: Walkers must book a fixed date and walk north to south in the peak season, which runs from October to May, and a track fee applies. Departure dates fill early, so book well ahead.

goodToKnow.title: Pack for all weather
goodToKnow.detail: Rain, wind and cold can arrive within minutes even in summer, so carry waterproofs and warm layers on every walk. Do not feed the wildlife, and keep food packed away because currawongs will open bags.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} bring the longest days and the mildest, most settled weather for the high walks, though rain is possible at any time. Autumn gives colour on the deciduous beech, and winter snow closes the high tracks to casual walkers.

name: Devonport
tagline: The Spirit of Tasmania ferry port, with a lighthouse headland, penguins and the coast and hills of the north-west.
description: Devonport is a regional city at the mouth of the Mersey River and the arrival point for the Spirit of Tasmania ferry from Victoria. Most visitors pass through on their way to Cradle Mountain, but the town has its own headland, museums and a penguin colony. Within a short drive are the mural town of Sheffield, a steam railway, limestone caves and canyon walks. A little penguin colony nests on the foreshore in the warmer months.
whyVisit: See little penguins at Lillico Beach
whyVisitSubjects: little penguins on Lillico Beach

goodToKnow.title: Ferry bookings
goodToKnow.detail: The Spirit of Tasmania links Devonport with Victoria, and vehicles need a booking in advance; check the operator's timetable as sailings differ by season.

goodToKnow.title: Penguin etiquette
goodToKnow.detail: Little penguins come ashore at dusk in the warmer months, from about October to March; keep your distance, use no flash and follow the viewing platform rules.

goodToKnow.title: Hire a car for the area
goodToKnow.detail: The caves, Sheffield and the Leven Canyon are out of town on country roads, so a car is the practical way to see them; allow a full day for the loop.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the warmest, and the penguins are on shore at dusk through the summer breeding season. Winter is cool and wet, though the hills and caves can still be visited.

name: Wynyard
tagline: A small north-west coast town beneath Table Cape, with tulip fields and quiet beaches.
description: Wynyard is a small town on the Inglis River where the coast road meets Bass Strait. The basalt headland of Table Cape rises behind it, with a lighthouse and fields that are planted with tulips for the spring bloom. To the west the road runs past Fossil Bluff and the coves of Boat Harbour and Sisters Beach into Rocky Cape National Park. It suits a slow day of coast and lookouts between Burnie and Stanley.

goodToKnow.title: Tulip season is short
goodToKnow.detail: The tulip farm at Table Cape blooms for a few weeks in spring and opens only then; check its dates before you drive out.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass for Rocky Cape
goodToKnow.detail: Rocky Cape National Park needs a valid Tasmanian parks pass for entry.

goodToKnow.title: Drive the coast
goodToKnow.detail: There is little public transport along this stretch, so plan to drive; fuel and food are easiest in Wynyard and Burnie.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} cover the tulip bloom in spring and the warm beach weather of summer. Winter is wild and wet on this exposed coast.

name: Burnie
tagline: A working port city on Bass Strait with penguins at the foreshore and gardens and falls inland.
description: Burnie is a regional port and industrial city on Tasmania's north-west coast, known for its paper mill and harbour. It is also a base for gentler outings: little penguins come ashore at Parsonage Point, and the Emu Valley garden and Guide Falls are a short drive south. The nearby town of Penguin has a giant penguin statue on its main street.

goodToKnow.title: Penguin viewing
goodToKnow.detail: Guided viewing at the observation centre runs at dusk from October to March; confirm opening times and tour arrangements before going.

goodToKnow.title: Falls are best after rain
goodToKnow.detail: Guide Falls flows best in winter and spring and can be modest after a dry summer.

goodToKnow.title: A car helps
goodToKnow.detail: The garden at Romaine and Guide Falls are a short drive out of town; there is little public transport beyond the main road.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} bring the penguin season and the best weather for the garden. Guide Falls runs strongest in winter and spring.

name: Mole Creek Karst National Park
tagline: Limestone country of show caves, glow-worms and cliff-edge lookouts below the Great Western Tiers.
description: Mole Creek Karst National Park was created to protect an underground landscape of caves, sinkholes, gorges and streams that run below the surface. Two show caves are open to visitors: Marakoopa, with its glow-worm display and the Great Cathedral cavern, and King Solomons, a compact, drier cave with shawls and stalactites. Above ground, a scenic drive through Chudleigh, Mole Creek and Caveside links the caves with Devils Gullet and the gateway town of Deloraine. Many lesser caves are reserved for recreational cavers.

goodToKnow.title: Cave tours are guided
goodToKnow.detail: Both show caves are visited on guided tours at set times; the Underground Rivers and Glow Worms tour and the King Solomons tour suit all ages, but the Great Cathedral tour needs medium fitness.

goodToKnow.title: Pass and tickets
goodToKnow.detail: A parks pass is not needed for the show caves themselves, but tour tickets are, and a pass lets you visit other scenic spots such as Croesus Reserve.

goodToKnow.title: Bring a jacket
goodToKnow.detail: Caves stay cool and damp all year, and the park can be cold and wet at any time.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} give the easiest driving and walking weather in the Tiers. The caves stay the same temperature year round, so winter visits work too.

name: King Island
tagline: A windswept Bass Strait island of lighthouses, shipwreck history, surf beaches, cheese and crayfish.
description: King Island lies in Bass Strait between Tasmania and Victoria, and visitors reach it by air from Melbourne or northern Tasmania; there is no ferry. Its coast has claimed many ships, which is why the island has an unusually tall lighthouse and several wreck memorials, and divers come for the wrecks. The pasture produces rich milk for dairy products such as brie and cheddar, and the island is also known for lobster. The island has no traffic lights and few roads, so a hire car or bicycle is the way to get around.

goodToKnow.title: Fly in
goodToKnow.detail: There is no ferry service, so book a flight to Currie from Melbourne, Burnie or Launceston with one of the small regional airlines, and book early in summer.

goodToKnow.title: Hire a car
goodToKnow.detail: Sights are spread across the island and there is little public transport; book a car or bicycle with your flights.

goodToKnow.title: Wind and wrecks
goodToKnow.detail: The west coast is exposed to strong swells and wind; stay back from cliff edges and follow the signs at wreck sites and lookouts.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the warmest and calmest, though wind is common year round. Winter brings storms and cold seas.

name: Flinders Island
tagline: Granite peaks, white beaches and quiet history in the Furneaux Group.
description: Flinders Island is the largest of the 78 islands in the Furneaux Group in Bass Strait, and one of two Bass Strait islands open to everyday tourism, with scheduled flights from Launceston and Melbourne. Granite peaks in Strzelecki National Park rise above white beaches and calm snorkelling water. The island also holds Wybalenna, where Aboriginal Tasmanians were exiled in the 1830s and 1840s, and a museum covering the sealers and shipwrecks of Bass Strait. Whitemark is its largest town, with about 300 people.

goodToKnow.title: Fly or sail
goodToKnow.detail: Flights run to Flinders Island Airport from Launceston and Essendon, and a freight boat sails from Bridport about weekly; check schedules with the operators.

goodToKnow.title: Rent a car
goodToKnow.detail: The B85 runs most of the island's length, and a hire car is the practical way to reach the peaks, beaches and Killiecrankie.

goodToKnow.title: Strzelecki is steep
goodToKnow.detail: The Strzelecki Peaks walk is a 4-5 hour return on a steep track; start early and carry water and a jacket.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the warmest, with the best weather for climbing, swimming and snorkelling. Winter is cool and windy.
